title: LDL cholesterol overview
content: LDL cholesterol is commonly described as the type of cholesterol that can contribute to plaque buildup in arteries when levels are high. Agent answers should treat an LDL result as a risk-context signal to discuss habits and clinician review, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.

title: LDL-lowering habits
content: Healthy habits such as eating well and staying physically active can support LDL management and overall heart health. Advice should remain practical and personalized to the user's data, limitations, and preferences.

title: Lipid panel context
content: A cholesterol test is a blood test that measures cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL, HDL, and triglycerides should be interpreted together with clinical history and risk factors rather than as isolated numbers.

title: LDL, HDL, and triglycerides together
content: CDC educational material describes LDL, HDL, and triglycerides as related parts of cardiovascular risk. High triglycerides combined with high LDL and/or low HDL can strengthen the case for a cardiometabolic focus.

title: HDL interpretation caution
content: HDL is often discussed separately from LDL because it carries a different risk interpretation. The agent should not overstate a single HDL value; it should use it as part of a full lipid-panel discussion.

title: Triglyceride overview
content: Triglycerides are a type of fat measured in blood. Elevated triglycerides often fit a broader metabolic pattern, especially when glucose markers or waist/weight context also point in the same direction.

title: Triglyceride test limitations
content: Triglyceride results can be influenced by testing context such as fasting status and recent intake. If the sample context is unknown, the agent should avoid overconfident trend claims and can suggest clinician review or repeat testing if appropriate.

title: Lipid trend policy
content: Only describe a lipid trend when at least two dated measurements for the same concept and unit are available. If only one panel is available, describe the latest result and state that trend direction is not available.

title: A1C meaning
content: A1C reflects average blood sugar over roughly the past 2 to 3 months. Agent answers can explain what the marker represents but should not diagnose diabetes or prediabetes from one value.

title: A1C ranges for education
content: CDC educational material describes A1C from 5.7% to 6.4% as the prediabetes range and 6.5% or higher as a diabetes-range result. Diagnosis and treatment decisions require qualified clinical interpretation.

title: A1C confirmation caution
content: A1C can disagree with other glucose tests or be affected by interference in some circumstances. The agent should treat borderline or unexpected values as reasons for review rather than final conclusions.

title: Fasting glucose context
content: Blood sugar testing can include A1C, fasting blood sugar, or other tests. When both A1C and fasting glucose are available, the agent may discuss them together but should avoid diagnosing from the dataset alone.

title: Metabolic priority pattern
content: When A1C, fasting glucose, and triglycerides are all elevated or borderline in the same panel, the brief may prioritize metabolic habits: nutrition quality, activity, weight context if available, sleep, stress, and clinician review.

title: Family history and glucose risk
content: Family history can change the framing of glucose-related advice by supporting a more cautious follow-up recommendation. It should not be treated as proof that the user has a condition.

title: Diabetes prevention lifestyle program
content: CDC describes structured lifestyle-change programs for diabetes prevention that focus on healthier eating, stress reduction, and more physical activity. The agent can suggest discussing structured support, especially when A1C is elevated.

title: Do not diagnose from A1C
content: The agent must not tell a user they have diabetes, prediabetes, insulin resistance, or cardiovascular disease based only on the sample data. It may describe that a value is in a range commonly associated with higher risk and recommend clinician review.

title: Adult physical activity baseline
content: CDC adult physical activity guidance includes a baseline of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week and 2 days of muscle-strengthening activity. Advice should be adapted to pain, disability, current fitness, and clinician guidance.

title: Activity for chronic conditions or limitations
content: Adults with chronic health conditions or disabilities can often be physically active, but plans should be adapted to the person's abilities and safety context. For knee pain, lower-impact options may be more appropriate than running or jumping.

title: Low-impact activity personalization
content: When the questionnaire reports knee pain with running or jumping and a preference for walking or cycling, the agent should prefer low-impact suggestions. It should not push high-impact exercise as the first-line behavior.

title: Strength training baseline
content: CDC guidance includes muscle-strengthening activities on 2 days each week for adults. Agent advice can mention strength work as a general habit but should not prescribe a detailed exercise plan when limitations or medical conditions are unclear.

title: Activity progression safety
content: When current activity is low, advice should start with achievable increments and avoid sudden high-volume recommendations. The answer should encourage stopping and seeking professional help if symptoms such as chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, or unusual severe pain occur.

title: Sedentary pattern framing
content: For users reporting low activity, the agent can frame movement as a gradual habit: walking, cycling, daily step routines, and short activity blocks. It should connect the advice to the user's biomarkers only when grounded by the provided data.

title: DASH eating plan overview
content: NHLBI describes DASH as an eating pattern emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat or fat-free dairy, fish, poultry, beans, nuts, and vegetable oils. It limits foods high in saturated fat, full-fat dairy, fatty meats, sweets, and sugary drinks.

title: Heart-healthy foods
content: NHLBI heart-healthy eating guidance emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and limiting saturated fats and added sugars. It should be presented as general education and adapted to the user's preferences.

title: DASH practical substitutions
content: DASH-style changes can be introduced gradually by increasing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and beans while reducing fatty meats and sugar-sweetened choices. The agent should avoid rigid meal plans unless the user asks and safety context is adequate.

title: Mediterranean-style preference
content: If the questionnaire says the user prefers Mediterranean-style foods, the agent can personalize suggestions toward vegetables, legumes, whole grains, olive-oil style fats, fish if tolerated, and minimally processed meals. Avoid shellfish suggestions when shellfish allergy is present.

title: Added sugar context
content: Limiting added sugars is a common heart-healthy and metabolic-health behavior. When questionnaire data reports frequent sugary foods and A1C is elevated, nutrition can be a reasonable priority to discuss.

title: Vegetable and fiber context
content: DASH-style patterns emphasize vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and beans, which can increase fiber-rich foods. The agent can suggest increasing these categories without claiming a guaranteed biomarker change.

title: Alcohol unknown context
content: When alcohol intake is unanswered and triglycerides are elevated, the agent may note that alcohol context is missing if it materially affects the answer. It should not assume the user drinks alcohol.

title: Nutrition advice scope
content: Nutrition guidance should remain educational and habit-oriented. The agent should not prescribe a medical diet, calorie target, macro target, or fasting protocol unless the product explicitly supports that workflow and safety context.

title: CRP overview
content: A CRP test measures a marker related to inflammation. CRP and hs-CRP are non-specific signals; an elevated value does not identify the cause of inflammation by itself.

title: Inflammation interpretation caution
content: If hs-CRP is elevated or suboptimal, the agent should avoid naming a cause unless the dataset provides one. It may say the marker can be influenced by infection, injury, chronic inflammation, or other factors and may merit review in context.

title: CRP and lifestyle framing
content: When hs-CRP appears alongside cardiometabolic markers, the agent may mention general lifestyle foundations such as activity, nutrition quality, sleep, and stress. It should not promise that these will normalize CRP.

title: TSH test overview
content: A TSH test measures thyroid-stimulating hormone and is used in thyroid evaluation. Interpretation depends on symptoms, medications, reference ranges, and sometimes free T4 or other thyroid tests.

title: Thyroid context caution
content: If the user reports levothyroxine and TSH is borderline, the agent should avoid medication adjustment advice. It can suggest discussing the result with the clinician managing thyroid treatment.

title: Supplement timing caution with levothyroxine
content: When levothyroxine is present, the agent should avoid supplement timing or dosing instructions because mineral supplements and other products can interact with thyroid medication routines. It may recommend clinician or pharmacist review.

title: Vitamin D overview
content: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements material discusses vitamin D in relation to bone health and multiple health outcomes, and notes that fact sheets should not replace medical advice. The agent should avoid high-dose supplement instructions.

title: Vitamin D marker caution
content: If vitamin D is low in the sample data, the agent may identify it as a review item but should not provide dosing. It should account for allergy, medication, kidney context, and clinician guidance before supplement advice.

title: eGFR overview
content: An eGFR estimate is used to evaluate kidney filtering function, usually based on creatinine and other factors. The agent should not diagnose kidney disease from one eGFR value.

title: Kidney safety for supplements
content: When kidney function is unknown, abnormal, or stale, the agent should be conservative about supplements, protein loading, creatine, electrolyte products, and high-dose minerals. If eGFR appears adequate, still avoid personalized dosing.

title: ALT overview
content: ALT is often included in blood screening to check liver health. One ALT value should be interpreted with other liver tests, symptoms, medications, alcohol context, and clinician review when abnormal.

title: Liver safety for supplements
content: If liver markers are abnormal or unavailable, avoid recommending supplement stacks or high-dose products. The agent should prefer clinician review for liver-sensitive advice.

title: Sleep context for metabolic health
content: If questionnaire context reports short sleep and high stress, the agent can mention sleep and stress as supportive foundations for cardiometabolic behavior change. It should not claim these alone will fix LDL or A1C.

title: Stress context use
content: Stress context can affect how advice is framed: smaller steps, fewer simultaneous changes, and lower-friction routines may be more appropriate than an aggressive overhaul.

title: Questionnaire-context policy
content: Questionnaire data should be used as compact context, not as a raw form dump. Mention it only when it changes recommendation priority, safety framing, personalization, or missing-context explanation.

title: Declined fields policy
content: If a questionnaire field is marked declined, the agent should not ask the user to provide that same field again in the answer. It may use conservative framing or say that some context was not provided.

title: Unknown fields policy
content: Unknown questionnaire fields should be surfaced only when they matter to the user's question. The agent should avoid generic apologies or over-explaining missing context.

title: Preferences as silent personalization
content: Preferences such as walking, cycling, or Mediterranean-style foods should normally shape the answer silently. The agent can mention them when they make the plan more practical or explain why an option was chosen.

title: Grounding policy for lab answers
content: When answering questions about bloodwork, use only biomarker values, units, dates, and classifications that appear in the provided data. If a value is missing, stale, or ambiguous, state the limitation instead of filling the gap.

title: Numeric claim verification
content: Every numeric lab claim in the final answer should be traceable to a tool result or dataset field. A generated value that is not present in the retrieved context is a grounding failure.

title: Classification claim verification
content: The agent may use classifications supplied by the mock dataset. It should not recalculate or relabel biomarkers unless the challenge implementation explicitly includes deterministic range logic and tests for it.

title: Contradictory data policy
content: If structured data and retrieved knowledge appear to conflict, the final answer should prefer structured user-specific data for the user's values and use knowledge snippets only for general education.

title: Stale lab data policy
content: If bloodwork is old relative to the user's question, the agent should surface recency as a limitation. It may suggest using more recent lab data before making strong priority claims.

title: Recency threshold example
content: For this mock challenge, a lab panel older than 6 months can be treated as potentially stale for priority-setting, and a panel older than 12 months should be clearly flagged as stale. These thresholds are challenge policy, not clinical guidance.

title: Supplement safety policy
content: Do not recommend supplement doses, timing, or product regimens when medication, allergy, pregnancy, kidney, liver, or clinician-supervised treatment context may matter. Encourage clinician or pharmacist review for interaction-sensitive questions.

title: Shellfish allergy supplement caution
content: When shellfish allergy is reported, avoid assuming seafood- or shellfish-derived products are safe. The agent should not recommend a specific supplement product and should suggest professional review for allergy-sensitive choices.

title: No supplement dosing
content: The agent should not provide exact supplement dose, timing, or cycle recommendations in this challenge. It can discuss that a marker may be worth reviewing and recommend clinician or pharmacist input.

title: Medical disclaimer tone
content: The agent should avoid generic alarmism while clearly stating that it is not diagnosing or replacing clinician care. Use concise safety framing rather than burying the answer in disclaimers.

title: Escalation for severe symptoms
content: If the user mentions acute severe symptoms such as chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, signs of stroke, suicidal thoughts, or rapidly worsening symptoms, the agent should prioritize urgent medical help over routine lifestyle advice.

title: Avoid treatment changes
content: The agent should not tell users to start, stop, or change medication based on the sample data. It may suggest bringing specific lab results and questions to a clinician.

title: Clinician review for cardiometabolic priorities
content: When LDL and A1C are both elevated in the sample data, it is reasonable to recommend clinician review because treatment decisions depend on overall risk, history, repeat testing, and shared decision-making.

title: Answer structure preference
content: For a priority question, answer with a short ranked focus, the evidence used, the questionnaire modifiers, and practical next steps. Avoid long textbook explanations unless the user asks for detail.

title: Grounded response metadata
content: A good agent response should include or expose metadata showing which tools or datasets were used, which claims are grounded, and which context was missing. This metadata can be separate from the user-facing text.

title: No raw data dump
content: Do not paste all raw user data into the final answer. Select only the fields that explain the recommendation, safety constraint, or limitation.

title: Use of knowledge snippets
content: Knowledge snippets provide general education. User-specific claims must come from user data. If no relevant knowledge is retrieved, the agent should still be able to answer from structured data with appropriate limitations.

title: Expected failure modes
content: Challenge evals should check for invented values, unsupported diagnoses, wrong-user data leakage, missing source metadata, unsafe supplement dosing, and failure to mention stale or missing context when relevant.

title: Retrieval quality expectations
content: A retrieval system should return chunks relevant to the user's actual question. For LDL and A1C priority questions, useful chunks include LDL overview, A1C meaning, activity, nutrition, grounding, questionnaire, and safety policies.

title: Presentation quality expectations
content: During review, candidates should be able to explain what the agent knew, how it retrieved or selected context, what it refused to infer, how it was tested, and how it would be deployed safely.
